extracted.intended_audience: aspiring or hobbyist comedy writers seeking books/resources on sketch and comedic writing
extracted.subtask_description: Choosing books and resources that teach the craft of comedy writing (especially sketch and single-performer formats) with a technical focus on premises, scene structure, character development, and scene 'game'. Excludes memoirs, improv manuals, and general scriptwriting guides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical breakdown of the writing process
rubrics_metrics.description: a technical breakdown of the writing process: how to break down premises, structure scenes, develop characters, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for books that explicitly teach how to analyze and construct comedic material: identifying premises, structuring scenes, and developing characters rather than only giving high-level advice or anecdotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covers scripted format
rubrics_metrics.description: covers scripted format, but essays or other styles are good too
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer resources that address scripted forms (sketches, stage, screen), though well-structured essays or other formats that teach craft are acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for solo/performance formats
rubrics_metrics.description: ideal product from this would look like a one-person show or podcast
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose material that can be adapted into a one-person show or spoken/audio formats (e.g., sketch-to-solo adaptation, joke-to-mono performance), rather than ensemble-only approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not primarily example collections
rubrics_metrics.description: less interested in example of great comedy writing
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid books that are mainly anthologies or collections of funny pieces without substantive instruction on method or craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not improv-focused
rubrics_metrics.description: less interested in books on improve [improv]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude resources centered on improvisational theater techniques if the goal is to produce scripted/rewritten material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not general script-writing guides
rubrics_metrics.description: less interested in books on general script writing
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid general screenwriting/playwriting manuals that do not address comedy-specific beats, timing, or joke mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not memoirs
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid comedian memoirs and career stories that provide inspiration but little practical instruction on craft and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covers creating comedy narratives for stage and screen
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating comedy narratives for stage and screen (recommended as broader-than-sketch, useful for stage/screen storytelling)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek books that teach how to build comedic narratives suitable for theatrical and filmed media, including pacing, plot and scene arcs specific to comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic comedy craft & structure
rubrics_metrics.description: goes over a lot of basic comedy craft & structure
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer titles that explicitly teach joke construction, comedic timing, setup/punch mechanics, scene escalation, and other structural elements; authors who provide frameworks or exercises are especially useful. (Example: 'How To Write Funny' by Scott Dikkers is cited for this.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Accompanying resources and courses
rubrics_metrics.description: books or authors that provide additional resources (websites, classes) and institutions offering remote learning in sketch comedy
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value materials linked to further learning: websites with exercises, transcripts, or institutional classes (e.g., The Second City remote classes, UCB training) to practice and deepen skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and heighten the 'game of the scene'
rubrics_metrics.description: the concept of 'game of the scene' — the unusual thing that is explored and heightened
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for instruction that teaches how to find the scene's 'game' (the oddity or comedic premise) and how to explore and heighten that element through escalation and repetition; UCB training materials are recommended for this analysis-focused approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use interviews/podcasts about craft as supplemental learning
rubrics_metrics.description: podcasts and interviews that discuss the craft of comedy writing and analyze jokes/working methods
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplement book learning with long-form interviews (e.g., The Comedian's Comedian, Good One, Tim Ferriss with Jerry Seinfeld transcript) which often reveal practical approaches, writer workflows, and real-world examples of joke/problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match resource to personal goals (hobbyist vs. professional)
rubrics_metrics.description: I want to do this purely for my own pleasure ... I have no desire to go pro
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select materials pitched at hobbyists or focused on craft development for personal projects rather than career-advancement, industry networking, or agents/production business advice.
